4.2. Some known results on the homology of the graph complex

We briefly review some key theorems on the homology of the graph complex.

Theorem 30.

(Willwacher [35]). The zeroth homology group H0​(𝒢​𝒞2)H_{0}(\mathcal{GC}_{2}) is isomorphic to the graded dual of the Grothendieck-Teichmüller Lie algebra 𝔤​𝔯​𝔱\mathfrak{grt} (equivalently, the graph cohomology group H0​(𝒢​𝒞2)H^{0}(\mathcal{GC}_{2}) is isomorphic, as a graded Lie algebra, to 𝔤​𝔯​𝔱\mathfrak{grt}).

Unfortunately not much is known about the structure of 𝔤​𝔯​𝔱\mathfrak{grt} except that it contains the so-called ‘motivic’ Lie algebra, which in turn governs the structure of motivic multiple zeta values.

Theorem 31.

The Lie algebra 𝔤​𝔯​𝔱\mathfrak{grt} contains a copy of a free Lie algebra

𝕃⁡(σ3,σ5,…)↪𝔤​𝔯​𝔱\mathbb{L}(\sigma_{3},\sigma_{5},\ldots)\hookrightarrow\mathfrak{grt}

with one generator σ2​k+1\sigma_{2k+1} in every odd degree 2​k+12k+1.

One can show that the elements σ2​k+1\sigma_{2k+1} are dual to the wheel classes W2​k+1W_{2k+1}. An open conjecture of Drinfeld’s is that 𝔤​𝔯​𝔱\mathfrak{grt} should be isomorphic to the free graded Lie algebra with one element in every odd degree ≥3\geq 3, i.e., the previous map is surjective.

Let ℳg\mathcal{M}_{g} denote the moduli space of curves of genus g>1g>1. Its cohomology has a mixed Hodge structure, and in particular a weight filtration.

Theorem 32.

[21]

Hn​(𝒢​𝒞2(g))≅H2​g+n−1​(L​ℳgtrop)≅gr6​g−6W​H4​g−6−n​(ℳg)H_{n}(\mathcal{GC}_{2}^{(g)})\cong H_{2g+n-1}(L\mathcal{M}_{g}^{\mathrm{trop}})\cong\mathrm{gr}^{W}_{6g-6}H^{4g-6-n}(\mathcal{M}_{g})

Putting the above results together implies that the top weight-graded pieces of the cohomology of the spaces ℳg\mathcal{M}_{g}, for g>1g>1, contain the free Lie algebra 𝕃⁡(σ3,σ5,…)\mathbb{L}(\sigma_{3},\sigma_{5},\ldots). This circle of ideas gives an application of the theory of multiple zeta values to topology.

It follows in particular that the dimension of gr6​g−6W​H6​g−6−n​(ℳg)\mathrm{gr}^{W}_{6g-6}H^{6g-6-n}(\mathcal{M}_{g}) grows exponentially fast in gg. Recently, Borinsky has shown [5], using methods of zero-dimensional quantum field theory, how to compute the Euler characteristic of 𝒢​𝒞2\mathcal{GC}_{2}. He deduces that the homology of 𝒢​𝒞2\mathcal{GC}_{2} in fact grows super-exponentially.

4.3. Questions arising

Question 33.

What is the precise relationship between H0​(𝒢​𝒞2)H_{0}(\mathcal{GC}_{2}) and multiple zeta values?

The results mentioned in the previous paragraph imply that H0​(𝒢​𝒞2)H_{0}(\mathcal{GC}_{2}) admits a map to the ring of multiple zeta values modulo products and modulo ζ⁡(2)\zeta(2). One expects that such a map should arise by associating an integral to a graph, along the lines discussed in §2. We shall explain how one can achieve this in more detail in the following lecture. A related question is whether one can associate motives to graph homology classes which would explain the appearance of the motivic Lie algebra in theorem 31. In degree zero, one would expect these to be mixed Tate motives over the integers.

Question 34.

How can we interpret the higher-degree homology Hn​(𝒢​𝒞2)H_{n}(\mathcal{GC}_{2}) for n>0n>0?

If indeed one can assign motives and period integrals to graph homology classes, what kinds of numbers should we expect from the higher-degree homology classes?

4.4. Differential forms on the moduli space of tropical curves

A first answer to question 33 was given in the work of Rossi-Willwacher, who defined integrals associated to graphs of the type arising in deformation quantisation. They used this to show that the wheel classes are non-zero in graph homology.

Since the graph complex computes the homology of the moduli space of tropical curves, a more geometric approach would be to define integrals directly on the space L​ℳgtropL\mathcal{M}_{g}^{\mathrm{trop}} of tropical curves, whose domains of integration are the simplices σG\sigma_{G}. However, in order to define the integrands, one needs a notion of differential form on these spaces, which we recall are not differentiable manifolds and, in addition, can have a local orbifold structure and therefore the usual de Rham theory does not apply.

The following definition, however, is adapted to these features.

Definition 35.

A differential nn form ω\omega on L​ℳgtropL\mathcal{M}_{g}^{\mathrm{trop}} is a family of differential forms

{ωG}G∈Cn​(σ¯G)\{\omega_{G}\}_{G}\ \in\ C^{n}(\overline{\sigma}_{G})

which are smooth on an open neighbourhood of σ¯G\overline{\sigma}_{G}, one for each stable weighted graph GG of genus gg, which satisfy the compatibility conditions

τ∗​ωG\displaystyle\tau^{*}\omega_{G} =\displaystyle= ωG for all ​τ∈Aut⁡(G)\displaystyle\omega_{G}\qquad\hbox{ for all }\tau\in\mathrm{Aut}(G)
ωG|σ¯G/e\displaystyle\omega_{G}\Big|_{\overline{\sigma}_{G/e}} =\displaystyle= ωG/e\displaystyle\omega_{G/e}

where the second condition means that the restriction of ωG\omega_{G} to the locus ℓe=0\ell_{e}=0 (which, we recall, is canonically identified with σ¯G/e\overline{\sigma}_{G/e}) coincides with ωG/e\omega_{G/e}.

Thus a differential form on L​ℳgtropL\mathcal{M}_{g}^{\mathrm{trop}} is a collection of forms ωG\omega_{G}, one for each cell σG\sigma_{G}, which glue together in a consistent manner.

One can try to construct examples of such differential forms recursively. Suppose that we have a differential form defined on all simplices of dimension <k<k. Then one can try to extend these forms to all simplices of dimension kk, and proceed by induction. The existence of such differential forms is guaranteed by a kind of de Rham theorem for spaces of this kind [17], but this procedure is not easy to carry out in practice.

Unfortunately, I do not presently know of an explicit general construction of differential forms on L​ℳgtropL\mathcal{M}_{g}^{\mathrm{trop}}. There is, however, a very natural construction of differential forms which are allowed poles along the boundary locus ∂L​ℳgtrop\partial L\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{trop}}_{g} which we shall describe in the next lecture. Such a form is to be interpreted, roughly speaking, as a differential form on the open locus L​ℳg∘,tropL\mathcal{M}_{g}^{\circ,\mathrm{trop}}.

4.5. Example

The idea is to use a graph Laplacian matrix ΛG\Lambda_{G} to define a differential form universally in GG, in such a way that it does not depend on the choice of cycle basis for H1​(G,ℤ)H_{1}(G;{\mathbb{Z}}) which is implicit in the definition of ΛG\Lambda_{G}.

In the case of the wheel with 3 spokes, we shall consider in the next lecture the canonical integral

∫σW3tr⁡((ΛW3−1​d​ΛW3)3)=∫σW310​ΩW3ΨW32=60​ζ​(3).\int_{\sigma_{W_{3}}}\mathrm{tr}\,\left((\Lambda_{W_{3}}^{-1}d\Lambda_{W_{3}})^{3}\right)=\int_{\sigma_{W_{3}}}10\frac{\Omega_{W_{3}}}{\Psi_{W_{3}}^{2}}=60\,\zeta(3)\ .

which happens in this case to reduce to a Feynman residue. Feynman residues themselves will not do: the integrands cannot be assembled to form a compatible system as they stand because the degree of the integrand of the Feynman residue of a graph GG depends on the number of edges in GG.

5. Canonical forms and general linear group

We now introduce a universal construction of differential forms associated to families of matrices, which will provide a canonical source of integrands compatible with all the structures considered so far. Applying this construction to the graph Laplacian matrices ΛG\Lambda_{G} will give well-defined differential forms which can be assembled together in the manner of the previous lecture. From this, we may define ‘canonical’ integrals on tropical moduli spaces of curves, which will enable us to make a connection between graph homology classes, Feynman integrals and multiple zeta values.

5.1. Bi-invariant forms

Let XX be an m×mm\times m matrix whose entries Xi​jX_{ij} we think of as generic functions. The differential d​XdX is the matrix whose entries are differential 11-forms

(d​X)i​j=d​Xi​j.(dX)_{ij}=dX_{ij}\ .

Consider the differential nn-form:

ωXn=tr⁡((X−1​d​X)n)∈ℚ⁡[Xi​j,d​Xi​j,1det(X)].\omega_{X}^{n}=\mathrm{tr}\,\left(\left(X^{-1}dX\right)^{n}\right)\quad\in{\mathbb{Q}}\!\left[X_{ij},dX_{ij},\frac{1}{\det(X)}\right]\ .

Since it involves inverting the matrix XX and has nn factors it a priori has denominator det(X)n\det(X)^{n}. One shows that for n=1n=1 one has:

ωX1=d​log​det(X)=d​det(X)det(X).\omega_{X}^{1}=d\log\det(X)=\frac{d\det(X)}{\det(X)}\ .
Example 36.

Consider a generic family of 2×22\times 2 matrices:

X=(x1x3x4x2)X=\begin{pmatrix}x_{1}&x_{3}\\ x_{4}&x_{2}\end{pmatrix}

The reason for the strange numbering is simply to make the signs easier to write down. One may check that

ωX3=tr(X−1dX.X−1dX.X−1dX)=3∑i=14(−1)ixi​d​x1∧…​d​xi^∧…​d​x4det(X)2\omega^{3}_{X}=\mathrm{tr}\,(X^{-1}dX.X^{-1}dX.X^{-1}dX)=3\sum_{i=1}^{4}(-1)^{i}\frac{x_{i}\,dx_{1}\wedge\ldots\widehat{dx_{i}}\wedge\ldots dx_{4}}{\det(X)^{2}}

A priori, we expect the power of det(X)\det(X) in the denominator to be 33, but there is a cancellation with a det(X)\det(X) which factors into the numerator. In the end, the power of det(X)\det(X) in the denominator is only two.

A remarkable feature of these forms is that, despite their definition, significant cancellations occur, resulting in much lower powers of det(X)\det(X) in the denominator than one might expect a priori.

Example 37.

Consider the symmetric matrix

X=(x1x4x5x4x2x6x5x6x3).X=\begin{pmatrix}x_{1}&x_{4}&x_{5}\\ x_{4}&x_{2}&x_{6}\\ x_{5}&x_{6}&x_{3}\end{pmatrix}\ .

Then one finds that ωX3=0\omega^{3}_{X}=0, and with the help of a computer, one may check that

(11) ωX5=10​∑i=15(−1)i​xi​d​x1∧…∧d​xi^∧…∧d​x6det(X)2\omega^{5}_{X}=10\sum_{i=1}^{5}(-1)^{i}\frac{x_{i}\,dx_{1}\wedge\ldots\wedge\widehat{dx_{i}}\wedge\ldots\wedge dx_{6}}{\det(X)^{2}}

Again, one sees that there are many cancellations: the power of det(X)\det(X) in the denominator is only two, whereas one would have expected it to be five.

5.2. Properties

The forms ωXn\omega_{X}^{n} have a number of remarkable properties. One shows as a simple consequence of the definition that they vanish if nn is even, and define closed forms otherwise: d​ωXn=0d\omega_{X}^{n}=0. Furthermore, one has

ωXTn=(−1)n⁡(n−1)2​ωXn\omega^{n}_{X^{T}}=(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}\omega^{n}_{X}

which implies that if XX is symmetric, then ωXn\omega^{n}_{X} vanishes for n≡3mod4n\equiv 3\mod 4. Finally, if n>1n>1 one has the projective invariance property

ωλ​Xn=ωXn\omega^{n}_{\lambda X}=\omega^{n}_{X}

for any λ\lambda (not necessarily constant). Note that this property fails for ωX1\omega^{1}_{X}, which satisfies ωλ​X1=ωX1+d​λλ\omega^{1}_{\lambda X}=\omega^{1}_{X}+\frac{d\lambda}{\lambda} and for this reason will be discarded.

We will typically consider symmetric matrices XX. Thus, after setting aside ωX1\omega^{1}_{X}, we have at our disposal an infinite sequence of closed differential forms:

ωX5,ωX9,ωX13,…\omega^{5}_{X},\omega^{9}_{X},\omega^{13}_{X},\ldots

The most important property of these forms are their bi-invariance.

Lemma 38.

Let XX be an invertible m×mm\times m matrix as above. For any invertible matrices A,B∈GLm​(ℝ)A,B\in\mathrm{GL}_{m}({\mathbb{R}}) with constant entries (i.e. d​A=d​B=0dA=dB=0), one has

ωXn=ωA​Xn=ωX​Bn.\omega^{n}_{X}=\omega^{n}_{AX}=\omega^{n}_{XB}\ .
Proof.

The form X−1​d​XX^{-1}dX is already invariant by left-multiplication by AA. Indeed,

(A​X)−1​d​(A​X)=X​A−1​A​d​X=X−1​d​X.(AX)^{-1}d(AX)=XA^{-1}A\,dX=X^{-1}dX\ .

It follows that ωXn\omega^{n}_{X} is also left-invariant. Now observe that d​X​X−1dXX^{-1} is invariant by right-multiplication by BB and notice that

ωXn=tr(X−1dX.…X−1dX)=tr(dXX−1.…dXX−1)\omega^{n}_{X}=\mathrm{tr}\,(X^{-1}dX.\ldots X^{-1}dX)=\mathrm{tr}\,(dXX^{-1}.\ldots dXX^{-1})

by cyclicity of the trace. ∎

The property of bi-invariance implies that

ωGn:=ωΛGn\omega^{n}_{G}:=\omega^{n}_{\Lambda_{G}}

is well-defined for any choice of graph Laplacian matrix ΛG\Lambda_{G} associated to GG. Indeed, changing cycle basis in the definition of ΛG\Lambda_{G} modifies ΛG\Lambda_{G} via the transformation

ΛG↦PT​ΛG​P for some ​P∈GLhG​(ℤ).\Lambda_{G}\mapsto P^{T}\Lambda_{G}P\qquad\hbox{ for some }P\in\mathrm{GL}_{h_{G}}({\mathbb{Z}})\ .

This implies that the forms ωG\omega_{G} associated to graph Laplacians are well-defined independently of the choice of cycle basis, and consequently glue consistently across the cells of the tropical moduli space.

5.3. Canonical integrals

Define the canonical algebra to be the graded exterior algebra

Ωcan∙=⋀(⨁k>0ℚ​ω4​k+1)\Omega^{\bullet}_{\mathrm{can}}=\bigwedge\left(\bigoplus_{k>0}{\mathbb{Q}}\omega^{4k+1}\right)

to be viewed as a formal graded algebra where ω4​k+1\omega^{4k+1} is in degree 4​k+14k+1. It is generated as a ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-vector space by

ω4​i1+1∧ω4​i2+1∧…∧ω4​ir+1\omega^{4i_{1}+1}\wedge\omega^{4i_{2}+1}\wedge\ldots\wedge\omega^{4i_{r}+1}

for all increasing sequences 1≤i1<i2<…<ir1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<\ldots<i_{r}. Each element ω∈Ωcan\omega\in\Omega_{\mathrm{can}} may be viewed as a map which assigns to any graph GG a differential form ωG\omega_{G}.

Definition 39.

Let GG be any connected graph with n+1n+1 edges and let ω∈Ωcann\omega\in\Omega^{n}_{\mathrm{can}} be of degree nn. Define the canonical integral to be

(12) IG​(ω)=∫σGωGI_{G}(\omega)=\int_{\sigma_{G}}\omega_{G}

Unlike Feynman residues, which may diverge due to boundary singularities, a striking feature of canonical forms is that they automatically compensate these divergences.

Theorem 40.

[16] The canonical integrals IG​(ω)I_{G}(\omega) are always finite.

Thus every canonical form ω∈Ωcann\omega\in\Omega^{n}_{\mathrm{can}} defines a map

I∙​(ω):{Connected graphs with n+1 edges}⟶ℝI_{\bullet}(\omega):\{\hbox{Connected graphs with $n+1$ edges}\}\longrightarrow{\mathbb{R}}

For any such ω\omega, it follows from the definition ωG=ωΛG\omega_{G}=\omega_{\Lambda_{G}} that

ω∈ℚ⁡[xe,d​xe,e∈EG]​[1det(ΛG)].\omega\ \in\ {\mathbb{Q}}\left[x_{e},dx_{e},e\in E_{G}\right]\left[\frac{1}{\det(\Lambda_{G})}\right]\ .

Recall that det(ΛG)=ΨG\det(\Lambda_{G})=\Psi_{G} is the graph polynomial. Thus we may write

(13) IG​(ω)=∫σGNGΨGk​ΩGI_{G}(\omega)=\int_{\sigma_{G}}\frac{N_{G}}{\Psi_{G}^{k}}\Omega_{G}

for some integer k>0k>0 and NG∈ℚ⁡[xe,e∈EG]N_{G}\in{\mathbb{Q}}[x_{e},e\in E_{G}] is a certain numerator polynomial in the edge variables xex_{e}. It has the magical quality that it compensates all the singularities arising from the denominator ΨG\Psi_{G}, which vanishes along certain boundary components of the domain of integration, as discussed earlier. Thus canonical integrals may be viewed as natural “regularisations” of Feynman integrals, in which the numerator is determined so as to cancel all boundary divergences.

In short, canonical integrals are generalised Feynman integrals with the extraordinary property that they are always finite, irrespective of the graph GG.

5.4. Examples

In the following examples, we shall compare and contrast canonical integrals with Feynman residues, which we recall are given by the formula

IGres=∫σGΩGΨG2I^{\mathrm{res}}_{G}=\int_{\sigma_{G}}\frac{\Omega_{G}}{\Psi_{G}^{2}}

and which are often infinite. These examples illustrate that canonical integrals are closely related to Feynman residues, but may differ by subtle correction terms which alter both convergence properties and the weights of the resulting periods. A key point is that canonical integrals associated to one graph may coincide with Feynman residues of a different graph, suggesting the existence of hidden equivalences between these integrals.

  1. (1)

    Let G=W3G=W_{3} be the wheel with 3 spokes. By the computation in example 37, the canonical form is proportional to the Feynman residue integrand in this case. Thus the canonical integral is a multiple of the Feynman residue, see §4.5.

  2. (2)

    Let G=W5G=W_{5} be the wheel with 5 spokes. Then with the help of a computer, one checks that the canonical form simplifies to two terms:

    ωW59=18​(ΩW5ΨG2+12​x1​x2​…​x5ΨW33​ΩW5)\omega^{9}_{W_{5}}=18\left(\frac{\Omega_{W_{5}}}{\Psi_{G}^{2}}+12\,\frac{x_{1}x_{2}\ldots x_{5}}{\Psi_{W_{3}}^{3}}\Omega_{W_{5}}\right)\,

    where the edge variables x1,…,x5x_{1},\ldots,x_{5} correspond to the five spokes of the wheel W5W_{5}. The first term is the Feynman residue form and its integral is finite:

    (14) IW5res=70​ζ​(7).I^{\mathrm{res}}_{W_{5}}=70\zeta(7)\ .

    The second term in brackets also converges and yields

    ∫σW512​x1​x2​…​x5ΨW33​ΩW5=70​(ζ⁡(5)−ζ⁡(7)).\int_{\sigma_{W_{5}}}12\,\frac{x_{1}x_{2}\ldots x_{5}}{\Psi_{W_{3}}^{3}}\Omega_{W_{5}}=70(\zeta(5)-\zeta(7))\ .

    Thus the ζ⁡(7)\zeta(7) term cancels out of the canonical integral and one obtains

    (15) IW5​(ω9)=1260​ζ​(5).I_{W_{5}}(\omega^{9})=1260\,\zeta(5)\ .

    Notice that the canonical integral (15) and Feynman residue (14) for W5W_{5} have different weights (55 and 77 respectively).

    Remark 41.

    It would be interesting to show directly that the canonical integral is proportional to the Feynman residue for the wheel with four spokes:

    IW5​(ω9)=18​IW4resI_{W_{5}}(\omega^{9})=18\,I^{\mathrm{res}}_{W_{4}}

    Thus the canonical integral is in fact a Feynman residue, but for a different graph! A more striking example of this phenomenon is discussed below.

  3. (3)

    For general canonical integrals of the canonical forms ωG4​k+1\omega_{G}^{4k+1} one can show that IG​(ω4​k+1)I_{G}(\omega^{4k+1}) vanishes unless GG has exactly hG=2​k+1h_{G}=2k+1 loops. We extend the definition of I∙​(ω)I_{\bullet}(\omega) linearly to define a map on linear combinations of graphs.

    Theorem 42.

    Let Ξ∈𝒢​𝒞2\Xi\in\mathcal{GC}_{2} be a linear combination of oriented graphs with gg loops and 4​k+24k+2 edges whose differential vanishes: d​Ξ=0.d\,\Xi=0. Then if the canonical integral IΞ​(ω4​k+1)I_{\Xi}(\omega^{4k+1}) is non-zero, [Ξ]∈H0​(𝒢​𝒞2)[\Xi]\in H_{0}(\mathcal{GC}_{2}) is non-zero in homology.

    It follows that the canonical integrals can detect graph homology cycles.

  4. (4)

    (General canonical wheel integrals).

    Theorem 43.

    [8] The canonical wheel integrals for g≥3g\geq 3 odd are

    IWg​(ω2​g−1)=g​(2​gg)​ζ​(g).I_{W_{g}}(\omega^{2g-1})=g\,\binom{2g}{g}\zeta(g)\ .

    The differential form ωWg2​g−1\omega_{W_{g}}^{2g-1} has the form

    (16) ∑k≥0ck​(x1​…​xgΨG)k​ΩGΨG2\sum_{k\geq 0}c_{k}\left(\frac{x_{1}\ldots x_{g}}{\Psi_{G}}\right)^{k}\frac{\Omega_{G}}{\Psi_{G}^{2}}

    for certain coefficients ck∈ℚc_{k}\in{\mathbb{Q}}, where x1,…,xgx_{1},\ldots,x_{g} are the edge variables corresponding to the internal spokes of GG. It is a generalised Feynman integral, but has lowest possible weight amongst integrals of the form (16) compared to the Feynman residues of the wheel graphs, which have highest possible weight amongst integrals of the form (16). The previous theorem has a number of geometric consequences, including the fact that the wheel classes [Wg][W_{g}] are non-zero in H0​(𝒢​𝒞2)H_{0}(\mathcal{GC}_{2}).

    More generally, Jean-Luc Portner has proven the following result in his thesis.

    Theorem 44.

    (Portner) Let GG be a connected graph with 4​k+24k+2 edges. Then the canonical integral

    IG​(ω4​k+1)I_{G}(\omega^{4k+1})

    is a (single-valued) multiple zeta value of weight 2​k+12k+1.

    In fact he proves that the canonical integral is proportional to the Rossi-Willwacher integrals, which gives another proof of theorem 43.

Next we turn to non-trivial exterior products of two or more canonical forms.

Example 45.

Let G=K6G=K_{6} denote the complete graph on six vertices. It has 15 edges. One can check with a computer that

ωK65∧ωK69=9!8​∏e∈EK6xeΨK63​ΩK6.\omega_{K_{6}}^{5}\wedge\omega_{K_{6}}^{9}=\frac{9!}{8}\,\frac{\prod_{e\in E_{K_{6}}}x_{e}}{\Psi_{K_{6}}^{3}}\,\Omega_{K_{6}}\ .

This graph has a huge number of divergent subgraphs and is therefore as bad as one can get from the point of view of the Feynman residue. Nevertheless, the integrand above is convergent and Borinsky and Schnetz were able to compute the canonical integral:

(17) IK6​(ω5∧ω9)=9!16​(360​ζ​(3,5)+690​ζ​(3)​ζ​(5)−29315​π8)I_{K_{6}}(\omega^{5}\wedge\omega^{9})=\frac{9!}{16}\left(360\,\zeta(3,5)+690\zeta(3)\zeta(5)-\frac{29}{315}\pi^{8}\right)
=9!16​(15​ζ​(3)​ζ​(5)−2596​IK3,4res),=\frac{9!}{16}\left(15\,\zeta(3)\zeta(5)-\frac{25}{96}I^{\mathrm{res}}_{K_{3,4}}\right)\ ,

where IK3,4resI^{\mathrm{res}}_{K_{3,4}} was the Feynman residue for the bipartite graph mentioned in Lecture 1. Thus once again we see that the canonical integral is closely related to a Feynman residue of a completely different graph. It is a challenge to prove this directly (for example, by integration by parts and application of Stokes’ theorem [16]).

Recall from lecture 1 that we do not expect all Feynman residues to be multiple zeta values. An obvious question can be vaguely phrased as follows:

Question 46.

Are all canonical integrals MZV’s, or are they more like Feynman residues (in which case they are not MZV’s)?

Note that there is a difference between evaluating a canonical integral for individual graphs as opposed to linear combinations of graphs which are closed in the graph complex 𝒢​𝒞2\mathcal{GC}_{2}. The former class of numbers is larger than the latter so the corresponding answers to the previous question may be different in both cases.

Example 47.

We know of an infinite family of non-explicit canonical integrals of wedge products ω4​i+1∧ω4​j+1\omega^{4i+1}\wedge\omega^{4j+1}. The statement is as follows:

Theorem 48.

[8] For all odd integers 3≤m<n3\leq m<n there exists a non-trivial closed element Ξm,n∈𝒢​𝒞2\Xi_{m,n}\in\mathcal{GC}_{2} with edge degree 2​m+2​n−12m+2n-1, such that

IΞm,n​(ω2​m−1∧ω2​n−1)=ζ⁡(m)​ζ​(n)I_{\Xi_{m,n}}(\omega^{2m-1}\wedge\omega^{2n-1})=\zeta(m)\zeta(n)

and [Ξm,n]∈Hkm,n​(𝒢​𝒞2)[\Xi_{m,n}]\in H_{k_{m,n}}(\mathcal{GC}_{2}) is non-zero in graph homology in some odd degree km,nk_{m,n} where 0<km,n<2​min⁡{m,n}−3.0<k_{m,n}<2\min\{m,n\}-3.

We do not know how to pin down the precise degree km,nk_{m,n}.

5.5. Picture

We can now revisit the earlier diagram of graph homology (or rather its dual, graph cohomology) and match non-zero classes with a canonical form whose corresponding integral is non-trivial. Since graph cohomology has a Lie algebra structure, we may take Lie brackets of such elements to obtain potentially more classes. See table 2.

Question 49.

Write down an explicit differential form on L​ℳ8tropL\mathcal{M}_{8}^{\mathrm{trop}} which represents the class [ω5,ω9][\omega^{5},\omega^{9}]. It should correspond to an automorphic differential form on GL8​(ℤ)\mathrm{GL}_{8}({\mathbb{Z}}) (see next chapter), and its associated canonical integral over the class in H0​(𝒢​𝒞2(8))H_{0}(\mathcal{GC}_{2}^{(8)}) should produce an irreducible MZV of weight 88 (such as ζ⁡(3,5)\zeta(3,5)).

5.6. Comments

We have now come full circle and shown how the seemingly disparate ideas of these four lectures are in fact closely interconnected.

We have so far encountered two a priori distinct non-linear representations of MZVs: on the one hand, Feynman residues, and on the other, canonical integrals. They appear to be related in a subtle way. The former arise in high-energy physics, where their mathematical interpretation remains far from clear. The latter are related to the cohomology of the even graph complex, and may be viewed as kinds of ‘volumes’ of cells in a moduli space of tropical curves. The Stokes relations on these spaces seem to relate the two, and indeed both are special cases of ‘generalised Feynman periods’. This points towards a geometric interpretation of Feynman periods in quantum field theory that can be formulated entirely in mathematical terms, without reference to the underlying physical theory.

6. Epilogue: Panorama and questions

This final section is slightly more advanced, and goes beyond what was covered in my four lectures. We explain how the constructions introduced above arise naturally in the context of the general linear group and its associated symmetric spaces, thereby linking the entire framework to classical results in arithmetic geometry. Along the way we discuss two more ‘non-linear’ interpretations for MZV’s.

We first discuss the tropical Torelli map which associates to a metric graph its graph Laplacian, thereby embedding a certain part of the moduli space of tropical curves into the symmetric space of positive definite matrices modulo the action of GLg​(ℤ)\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{Z}}). Under this map, the canonical forms on matrices pull back to the forms constructed earlier on tropical moduli spaces, showing that the latter are manifestations of invariant differential forms on locally symmetric spaces. From this perspective, multiple zeta values arise as periods associated to the cohomology of arithmetic groups.

6.1. Tropical Torelli map, general linear group and algebraic K-theory

The canonical integrals have a natural geometric interpretation. There is a map, called the tropical Torelli map:

λ:ℳg∘,trop⟶Pg/GLg​(ℤ)\lambda:\mathcal{M}_{g}^{\circ,\mathrm{trop}}\longrightarrow P_{g}/\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{Z}})

which sends a marked metric graph GG to the class [ΛG]{[}\Lambda_{G}] of the graph Laplacian

The space PgP_{g} is the space of positive-definite symmetric matrices XX, where P∈GLg​(ℤ)P\in\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{Z}}) acts via

X↦PT​X​P.X\mapsto P^{T}XP\ .

Thus the equivalence class [ΛG]{[}\Lambda_{G}] in the quotient Pg/GLg​(ℤ)P_{g}/\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{Z}}) is well-defined88 8 The tropical Torelli map may be interpreted as the tropicalisation of the map which to a compact Riemann surface CC of genus gg associates its Riemann polarisation form. This is the g×gg\times g matrix whose i,ji,jth entry is 12​π​i​∫C⁡(ℂ)ωi∧ω¯j\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{C({\mathbb{C}})}\omega_{i}\wedge\overline{\omega}_{j} where ω1,…,ωg\omega_{1},\ldots,\omega_{g} are a basis for the holomorphic differentials on CC. .

The canonical forms X↦ωXX\mapsto\omega_{X}, for any ω∈Ωcan\omega\in\Omega_{\mathrm{can}} define closed differential forms on PgP_{g} which are invariant for the action of GLg​(ℤ)\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{Z}}). Borel famously computed the stable cohomology of the GLg​(ℤ)\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{Z}}) in the 1970’s. His result may be rephrased as saying that the natural map

(18) Ωcan∙⊗ℚℝ⟶lim←g⁡H∙​(Pg/GLg​(ℤ),ℝ)\Omega^{\bullet}_{\mathrm{can}}\otimes_{{\mathbb{Q}}}{\mathbb{R}}\longrightarrow\varprojlim_{g}H^{\bullet}(P_{g}/\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{Z}});{\mathbb{R}})

is an isomorphism. In other words, the stable cohomology of the general linear group GLg​(ℤ)\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{Z}}) is exactly given by the canonical bi-invariant forms. This builds on important prior work of Matsushima and Garland; Borel’s contribution was to prove the injectivity of (18) in very small degrees by studying the asymptotic growth of differential forms as they approach the boundary of PgP_{g}99 9 A much stronger version of this result [17] can be proven using the ideas discussed in these notes. An important corollary of Borel’s theorem is his computation of the rank of the algebraic KK-theory of the integers:

Kn​(ℤ)⊗ℤℚ≅{ℚ if n≡1(mod4) and n>10 otherwiseK_{n}({\mathbb{Z}})\otimes_{{\mathbb{Z}}}{\mathbb{Q}}\cong\begin{cases}{\mathbb{Q}}\quad\hbox{ if }n\equiv 1\pmod{4}\hbox{ and }n>1\\ 0\qquad\hbox{ otherwise}\end{cases}

This result is the lynchpin upon which the entire motivic theory of multiple zeta values depends: it explains the fact that the relations between multiple zeta values are governed by a free Lie algebra in odd degrees σ3,σ5,…\sigma_{3},\sigma_{5},\ldots, which are in one-to-one correspondence with the forms ω5,ω9,…\omega^{5},\omega^{9},\ldots.

The canonical forms associated to graphs are simply the pull-backs of the bi-invariant forms, which naturally live on Pg/GLg​(ℤ)P_{g}/\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{Z}}), by the Torelli map:

ωG=(λ∗​ω)|σG\omega_{G}=(\lambda^{*}\omega)\big|_{\sigma_{G}}

for any ω∈Ωcann.\omega\in\Omega^{n}_{\mathrm{can}}.

6.2. * Volumes, canonical Voronoi integrals, regulators

We briefly discuss the non-linear representations of zeta values as volumes of locally symmetric spaces and regulators, as mentioned in the introduction.

6.2.1. Volumes

First, we discuss a classical computation due to Minkowski, who calculated the covolume of GLg​(ℤ)\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{Z}}) inside GLg​(ℝ)\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{R}}) as a product of consecutive zeta values.

Theorem 50.

Let g>1g>1 be odd. Then

vo​lg=ω5∧ω9∧…∧ω2​g−1\mathrm{vo}l_{g}=\omega^{5}\wedge\omega^{9}\wedge\ldots\wedge\omega^{2g-1}

is a non-zero GLg​(ℝ)\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{R}})-invariant volume form on ℝ>0×\Pg{\mathbb{R}}^{\times}_{>0}\backslash P_{g}. There exists a non-zero rational number αg\alpha_{g} such that the volume

∫ℝ>0×\Pg/GLg​(ℤ)volg=αg​ζ​(3)​ζ​(5)​…​ζ​(g)\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{\times}_{>0}\backslash P_{g}/\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{Z}})}\mathrm{vol}_{g}=\alpha_{g}\,\zeta(3)\zeta(5)\ldots\zeta(g)

The first part of this theorem uses results on invariant theory to show that the exterior product of the canonical forms ω5∧…∧ω2​g−1\omega^{5}\wedge\ldots\wedge\omega^{2g-1} is indeed non-zero. The second part can be deduced from Minkowski’s theorem. In particular, we deduce yet another non-linear integral representation for ζ⁡(3)\zeta(3):

∫ℝ>0×\P3/GL3​(ℤ)ω5=α3​ζ​(3).\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{\times}_{>0}\backslash P_{3}/\mathrm{GL}_{3}({\mathbb{Z}})}\omega^{5}=\alpha_{3}\,\zeta(3)\ .

It turns out to be completely equivalent to the canonical integral IW3​(ω5)I_{W_{3}}(\omega^{5}) and the Feynman residue IW3resI^{\mathrm{res}}_{W_{3}}. The volume computation of Minkowski was generalised by Siegel to all number fields.

6.2.2. Voronoï decomposition

Much of the story we have discussed for the moduli space of tropical curves can be adapted to the setting of the locally symmetric space ℝ>0×\Pg/GLg​(ℤ){\mathbb{R}}^{\times}_{>0}\backslash P_{g}/\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{Z}}) for the general linear group. It too admits a cellular decomposition, due to Voronoï, which is analogous to the decomposition of L​ℳgtropL\mathcal{M}_{g}^{\mathrm{trop}} into simplices σG\sigma_{G}.

We briefly discuss some key ideas and refer to the excellent paper [7] for further details.

Definition 51.

Voronoï’s construction of a cellular decomposition of PgP_{g} is as follows. Each cell is indexed by a positive definite quadratic form

Q⁡(x,y)=∑1≤i,j≤gai​j​xi​yjQ(x,y)=\sum_{1\leq i,j\leq g}a_{ij}x_{i}y_{j}

where x,y∈ℝgx,y\in{\mathbb{R}}^{g} are column vectors of length gg. It may be written Q⁡(x,y)=xT​A​yQ(x,y)=x^{T}Ay where A=(ai​j)i​jA=(a_{ij})_{ij} is a positive definite symmetric matrix (i.e., one has Q⁡(x,x)≥0Q(x,x)\geq 0 with equality if and only if x=0x=0). To any such QQ one writes down the set of minimal vectors

MQ={ξ∈ℤg∖{0}:Q(ξ,ξ)≤Q(z,z) for all z∈ℤg∖{0}}M_{Q}=\{\xi\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{g}\setminus\{0\}:Q(\xi,\xi)\leq Q(z,z)\quad\hbox{ for all }z\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{g}\setminus\{0\}\}

which is a finite set of vectors in ℤg{\mathbb{Z}}^{g}. The cell associated to QQ is then the convex hull

CQ=ℝ>0⟨ξξT:ξ∈MQ⟩C_{Q}={\mathbb{R}}_{>0}\langle\xi\xi^{T}:\xi\in M_{Q}\rangle

where ξ​ξT\xi\xi^{T} are the symmetric rank 1 matrices whose i,ji,jth entries are ξi​ξj\xi_{i}\xi_{j}, where ξi\xi_{i} are the coordinates of a given minimal vector ξ∈MQ\xi\in M_{Q}. We denote by

σQ=ℝ>0×\CQ\sigma_{Q}={\mathbb{R}}^{\times}_{>0}\backslash C_{Q}

the corresponding quotient by the multiplicative scalar action of ℝ>0{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}.

Example 52.

Consider the quadratic form for g=2g=2 given by Q⁡(x,x)=x12+2​x1​x2+x22Q(x,x)=x^{2}_{1}+2x_{1}x_{2}+x_{2}^{2}. It has six minimal vectors

MQ={(x1,x2)=(±1,0),±(1,−1),(0,±1)}.M_{Q}=\{(x_{1},x_{2})=(\pm 1,0),\pm(1,-1),(0,\pm 1)\}\ .

The corresponding symmetric matrices ξ​ξT\xi\xi^{T} for ξ∈MQ\xi\in M_{Q} are of the form

{(1000),(1−1−11),(0001)}.\left\{\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix}\quad,\quad\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\ -1&1\end{pmatrix}\quad,\quad\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}\right\}\ .

Their convex hull consists of linear combinations of these three matrices with positive real coefficients:

CQ={(λ1+λ2−λ2−λ2λ1+λ3): for λ1,λ2,λ3>0}C_{Q}=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}&-\lambda_{2}\\ -\lambda_{2}&\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{3}\end{pmatrix}:\hbox{ for }\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}>0\right\}

The above matrix is nothing other than the graph Laplacian for the sunrise graph (8).

The set of cells σQ\sigma_{Q} as QQ ranges over all positive definite quadratic forms QQ decomposes the space ℝ>0×∖Pg{\mathbb{R}}^{\times}_{>0}\setminus P_{g} into polyhedral cells with the property that any distinct two such cells are either disjoint, or meet in a common face. Furthermore, this decomposition is equivariant with respect to the action of GLg​(ℤ)\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{Z}}) and thus, one may show, gives a finite cell decomposition of ℝ>0×∖Pg/GLg​(ℤ){\mathbb{R}}^{\times}_{>0}\setminus P_{g}/\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{Z}}).

One can prove [1] that the tropical Torelli map sends cells σG\sigma_{G} onto cells of the form σQ\sigma_{Q}. The following theorem is a generalisation of theorem 40.

Theorem 53.

[17] Let ω∈Ωcand\omega\in\Omega^{d}_{\mathrm{can}} and let σQ\sigma_{Q} be a Voronoï cell of dimension d−1d-1. Then the ‘canonical Voronoï’ integral

IQ​(ω)=∫ℝ>0×∖σQωI_{Q}(\omega)=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}^{\times}\setminus\sigma_{Q}}\omega

is finite.

Let g>1g>1 be odd. Recall that volg=ω5∧…∧ω2​g−1\mathrm{vol}_{g}=\omega^{5}\wedge\ldots\wedge\omega^{2g-1} is a volume form. By decomposing the fundamental domain into top-dimensional Voronoï cells σQ1,…,σQN\sigma_{Q_{1}},\ldots,\sigma_{Q_{N}} we deduce that

αg​ζ​(3)​ζ​(5)​…​ζ​(g)=∫ℝ>0×\Pg/GLg​(ℤ)volg=∑i=1NIQi​(volg)\alpha_{g}\zeta(3)\zeta(5)\ldots\zeta(g)=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{\times}_{>0}\backslash P_{g}/\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{Z}})}\mathrm{vol}_{g}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}I_{Q_{i}}(\mathrm{vol}_{g})

where the left-hand equality follows from Minkowski’s theorem. Thus the product of zeta values may be broken up as a sum of volumes of Voronoï cells.

Question 54.

What kinds of numbers can appear as volumes IQi​(volg)I_{Q_{i}}(\mathrm{vol}_{g})?

Example 55.

For g=3g=3, the space ℝ>0×\P3/GL3​(ℤ){\mathbb{R}}^{\times}_{>0}\backslash P_{3}/\mathrm{GL}_{3}({\mathbb{Z}}) has a single cone in its Voronoï decomposition, which is the image of the wheel W3W_{3}. Thus we retrieve, once more, the fact that the wheel canonical integral is proportional to ζ⁡(3)\zeta(3).

The space ℝ>0×\P5/GL5​(ℤ){\mathbb{R}}^{\times}_{>0}\backslash P_{5}/\mathrm{GL}_{5}({\mathbb{Z}}) has exactly 3 cones in its Voronoï decomposition. See [7, 25] for a precise description. One of them is the image of the cell σK6\sigma_{K_{6}} corresponding to the complete graph with 66 vertices. The fact that its canonical integral involves a non-irreducible multiple zeta value of weight 8 (namely ζ⁡(3,5)\zeta(3,5), see (17)) gives an arithmetic way to see that it cannot be the only such cell.

What are the volumes of the two other cones?

6.2.3. Regulators

For all k≥1k\geq 1, Borel defined the regulator

r4​k+1:K4​k+1​(ℤ)⊗ℤℚ⟶ℂr_{4k+1}:K_{4k+1}({\mathbb{Z}})\otimes_{{\mathbb{Z}}}{\mathbb{Q}}\longrightarrow{\mathbb{C}}

and proved that its image is the line ℚ​ζ​(2​k+1){\mathbb{Q}}\zeta(2k+1). It follows from our earlier interpretation of the stable cohomology of the general linear group that it is computed by the integral of the canonical form ω4​k+1\omega^{4k+1} over a certain locally finite homology class for GLg​(ℤ)\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{Z}}) where gg is sufficiently large (in the stable range). In particular, it is a linear combination of integrals of the form described in theorem 53. This computation is not only the origin of the non-triviality of the ‘motivic’ Soule elements σ2​k+1\sigma_{2k+1}, but also the reason for the appearance of odd zeta values in the theory of mixed Tate motives.

Remark 56.

A subtle fact is that regulators are periods of the stable cohomology of GLg​(ℤ)\mathrm{GL}_{g}({\mathbb{Z}}), and not immediately related to the wheel classes, which are dual to compactly supported cohomology classes, and which in any case lie outside the stable range. There is a subtle way to relate the two which is explained in [8] §2.4. For example, the first regulator map on K5K_{5} may be shown to be the quotient of a volume integral by a wheel integral

Im⁡(r5)=vol⁡(ℝ>0×\P7/GL7​(ℤ))IW5​ℚ=ζ⁡(3)​ζ​(5)ζ⁡(5)​ℚ=ζ⁡(3)​ℚ\mathrm{Im}(r_{5})=\frac{\mathrm{vol}({\mathbb{R}}^{\times}_{>0}\backslash P_{7}/\mathrm{GL}_{7}({\mathbb{Z}}))}{I_{W_{5}}}{\mathbb{Q}}=\frac{\zeta(3)\zeta(5)}{\zeta(5)}{\mathbb{Q}}=\zeta(3){\mathbb{Q}}

6.3. Concluding remarks and questions

There are two main sources for the appearance of multiple zeta values and mixed Tate motives in mathematics and physics. The first arises from linear geometry (relating to the fact that projective spaces have cohomology of Tate type) and appears in the context of hyperplane configurations, and in particular moduli spaces of curves of genus 00 with nn marked points ℳ0,n\mathcal{M}_{0,n}. At the core of this theory lies the unipotent fundamental group of the projective line minus three points, ℙ1∖{0,1,∞}\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{0,1,\infty\} [24].

The second arises from a ‘non-linear’ geometry associated with singular determinant loci. As we have explained, these arise in the context of Feynman integrals in quantum field theory, as canonical integrals on moduli spaces of tropical curves, and on the locally symmetric spaces of the general linear group GLn​(ℤ)\mathrm{GL}_{n}({\mathbb{Z}}). The latter are closely related to the theory of regulators in algebraic KK-theory. We expect that all multiple zeta values (or certainly a generating family modulo ζ⁡(2)\zeta(2)) naturally arise as integrals on these spaces, and that, in a suitable sense, the category of mixed Tate motives over ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} can be generated geometrically from a cell decomposition of the locally symmetric spaces for GLn​(ℤ)\mathrm{GL}_{n}({\mathbb{Z}}).

The examples discussed in these notes suggest that multiple zeta values are governed by a common geometric framework based on determinantal structures, which encompasses both the classical linear theory and the non-linear constructions arising in quantum field theory and arithmetic geometry. A central problem is to make this framework explicit, by identifying a direct geometric relationship between the linear and non-linear representations and thereby clarifying the unity underlying these apparently different constructions.
